Mr. R. B. HANSON (York-Sunbury) presented the second and final report of the select standing committee on privileges and elections, as follows:
Your committee have had before them an order of reference of the house under date of June 4, 1931, namely:
"That all correspondence and other communications in the possession of the government relating to the preparation of the voters' list for the municipality of Port McNicoll, in the riding of East Simeoe, and a copy of the original list prepared by the enumerator, and of the revised list as prepared by him for use on election day, together with a copy of any communications exchanged between the chief electoral officer and the returning officer or any other person as to the conduct of the poll on election day, laid on the table of the house 22110-2431
on Wednesday, the 27th of May, 1931, be referred to the select standing committee on privileges and elections with instructions to inquire fully into the registration and polling of the votes or other related matter in connection with the election in the electoral division of East Simeoe, on July 28, 1930."
Your committee have inquired into the matters referred to them under the terms of the above reference and have held five meetings in the course of which they have heard twelve witnesses. After having perused the evidence adduced before them, your committee beg leave to report as follows:
That in the opinion of the committee, having regard to the fact that it is the intention of the Dominion Elections Act to enfranchise as many voters as possible under the residence provisions if they have the other qualifications, those in situations similar to that of Messrs. Chidwick and Campbell, should have been entitled to vote.
Your committee therefore recommend that the necessary amendments be made to the Dominion Elections Act to enable persons similarly situated to vote at future Dominion elections.
Your committee also recommend that the proceedings and evidence, a copy of which is submitted herewith for the information of parliament, be printed as an appendix to the journals of the house for the present session.

C. S. Gzowski, chief engineer of construction, Canadian National Railways;

Canadian National Railways Bill 79
Your committee have had under consideration Bill 79. "An act respecting the Canadian National Railways and to authorize the expenditures made and indebtedness incurred during the calendar year 1931" amounting to $68,500,000 and have agreed to report the same without amendment.
Bill 83
Your committee have also had under consideration Bill 83, "An act respecting the Canadian National Railways and to authorize the guarantee by His Majesty of securities to be issued under the Canadian National Railways Financing Act, 1931" and beg leave to report the same without amendment.
The committee have considered the general report of last year's operations of the railway made by Sir Henry Thornton as president of the company and chairman of the board of directors and were partioidarly interested in his expressed intention to reduce the expenditures on capital account and wherever possible «n operation and maintenance. Yout committee heartily approve of such proposed action and recommend that for the present projects entailing capital expenditure be curtailed as far as possible.
Your committee desire to call the attention of the bouse to the proposal made by Sir Henry Thornton at one of the sessions of the committee. He referred to the serious position of the transportation business generally and recommended that a commission be appointed for the purpose of considering the whole question of Canadian transportation. Your committee regard such a recommendation coming from such a source at this time as worthy of the serious consideration of the government.
Canadian Government Merchant Marine
Your committee have had under consideration item 379 of the estimate's-loan to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited, to be applied in payment of deficits in operation of the company and of the vessels under the company's control during the year ending December 31, 1931, amounting in all to $588,500.
Your committee also reviewed the balance sheet of the company and are of the opinion that the amount of $588,500 included under item 379 of the estimates, is required for the purposes of the company and should be granted by this house.
Your committee believe that the time has come when the government should very carefully consider the abandonment of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, and the making of arrangements with other shipping companies so that the external trade of Canada will not be jeopardized. In this respect we wish to point out that the total original cost of this
(Mr. Chaplin.]
enterprise which was undertaken solely as a result of the exigencies of the war was approximately $80,000,000.
After almost ten years of operation there has not been a single year in which an operating profit has been shown by the merchant marine.
Throughout the whole period, a deficit of over $57,000,000 has accumulated, including depreciation on ships sold and interest due the government, but does not include accrued depreciation on vessels remaining in the fleet, which depreciation amounts to more than $17,000,000 in addition. Your committee has been informed that the ships are for the most part obsolete and only part of the fleet is now in operation.
Canadian National (West Indies) Services
Your committee have had under consideration item 380, loan to the Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships, Limited, whose steamships provide the services called for by the West Indies Trade Agreement.
Your committee note that the operations for the year ending December 31, 1930, resulted in an operating loss of $523,136.98, which is partly offset by the fact that previously a subsidy equial to $380,000 per annum was paid to a private company by the Dominion government for a similar service.
Your committee further believe that the steamship service established on the Pacific coast and known as the Triangular Service between Vancouver, Seattle, and Victoria should not have been established as it does not earn its operating expenses. We, therefore, recommend that serious consideration be given to immediate action looking toward the elimination of this loss.
Maritime Freight Rates Act
Your committee have also had under consideration item 382 of the estimates, to provide for the payment to the Canadian National Railway Company as required by the Maritime Freight Rates Act, of the deficit incurred during 1931 on eastern lines, the amount of the estimated deficit being $6,631,856, and in addition the sum of $2,450,632, representing the estimated amount by which the revenues of the eastern lines will be lessened during the coming year by the reduced rates granted under the Maritime Freight Rates Act in accordance with the recommendations of the Duncan commission.
By reason of the special consideration involved in the maritime railway situation, with which the house is familiar, your committee are of the opinion that these amounts are necessary to give effect to the Maritime Freight Rates Act in the operation of the eastern lines.
Your committee have -also had under consideration item 381, to provide the sum of $900,000 from which privately owned railways operating in territory eoveTed by the Maritime Freight Rates Act shall be reimbursed the difference between normal tolls and special tolls provided by that act. Your committee are of the opinion that this amount is necessary to implement the provisions of the act in that regard and should be granted by this house.
Certain questions relating to the salaries and emoluments paid to executive officers of the company were asked by members of the committee. and were by resolution of the committee submitted to a sub-committee for consideration. The report of the sub-committee has been re-

ceived accompanied by a statement from the president of all salaries of $15,000 per annum and over, together with the names of the officials receiving them. The president, Sir Henry Thornton, has expressed the opinion that it is not in the best interests of the railway that the list of such salaries and the names of the recipients be published.
Your committee, while of opinion that many of the salaries are much too generous, and in some instances excessive, accede to the expressed wish of the president that the list be not published for the reasons given by him.
Your committee, however, are of opinion that the salary of the president stands on a different footing as he 'has a term contract calling for the payment of $75,000 per annum from the National Railways and all its subsidiaries, besides legitimate out of pocket expenses, which wras negotiated by the previous government and approved by order in council. Therefore, to all intents and purposes the salary of the president is a matter of contract with the Dominion of Canada and is a public document.
Your committee also are informed that in addition to the contractual salary of the president above referred to, he is, with the approval of the former board of directors, in receipt of other substantial amounts in the form of salary and emoluments, which he receives in addition to his contractual salary.
It has also come to the knowledge of your committee that the late board of directors in the year 1929 passed a resolution recommending the payment of an annuity of $30,000 per annum for life to Sir Henry Thornton, if his services to the railway Should at any time be terminated. Your committee are of opinion that such resolution was unnecessary and should be rescinded forthwith. If later on the services of Sir Henry Thornton are discontinued and his contract terminated, the matter of a retiring allowance may then be discussed on its merits, by the directors and the government.
In view of the decreased revenues of the company, and the economies being made in other branches of the service, your committee are of the opinion that the executive committee of the board of directors should immediately consider the whole question of salaries, allowances, disbursements, pensions and retirement previsions for executive officers and officials of the company, receiving salaries of $5,000 and over in order that every reasonable and proper economy should be effected.	#
Your committee recommend thiat immediate action be taken in these matters and a report be made to the select standing committee on railways and shipping, owned, operated and controlled by the government, at the next session of parliament.
Your committee strongly condemn the practice which has grown up under which the National railways are chargeable with large amounts for payment for the social entertainment and other activities of officials on other than official business. Your committee recommend that this practice should be discontinued forthwith. Expenditures for such purposes are in the opinion of your committee, wrong in principle and practice, and should never have been permitted.
When it is necessary in the interest of the business of the railway that moneys should be expended chargeable to the railway for entertainment, then it should be approved by the executive committee.
In reporting the result of the conferences of the committee with the president and officials of the railway, your committee would draw the attention of parliament to the magnitude of the task wdiieh was referred to them by the house. In the opinion of your committee, it is a practical impossibility to conduct an exhaustive inquiry into the affairs and management of the Canadian National Railways and Mercantile Marine within the time at the disposal of the committee. The result of the partial investigation conducted by the committee is by no means adequate, complete or satisfactory. Full justice cannot he done in respect, of an undertaking of so great magnitude without much greater time than the committee had at their disposal. The committee desire to emphasize this phase of the matter to the house, and recommend that in order that the operations of the company be fully scrutinized, a thorough audit by an independent auditor, appointed by the government, should be made from time to time of all such matters and accounts as may be designated by the minister.' and reported to him.	-

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
subtopic: PROGRESS OF WORK AT CHURCHILL-POSSIBILITY OF TEST SHIPMENTS OF GRAIN THIS SEASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Bowman) asked a question yesterday in connection with the progress of the work at Churchill, and the possibility of shipping grain this season out of that port. I promised the hon. member that I would make a statement to-day.
I stated then, and I repeat now, that the work of developing the port is ahead of schedule, and there is no doubt but that by September 15, the date upon which the elevator is to be finished under the terms of the contract signed by the late minister, the elevator will be available. My officials state that the four-year construction program of the late government contemplated a test of facilities this coming autumn, and the completion of the port during the season of 1932.
As the responsible minister, I have taken every opportunity to press forward the work

Hudson Bay Railway
and we have reached the point where, barring accident, we will be in a position to handle sufficient grain out of Churchill between September 15 this year and the close of navigation to demonstrate the feasibility of the project.
There has been discussion in the press of western Canada as to the quantity of grain that should be handled in this test movement. I have made careful inquiry of my departmental officials, and the records have also been searched, and I am unable to find any statement as to quantity of grain to be moved in connection with the proposed test of terminal facilities. I am advised toy officials of the department who 'have been constantly in touch with the matter that, in view of the necessity as far as possible to avoid interference with the dredging and construction program, it was never contemplated that more than two or three cargoes should be attempted in this test movement. Pending organization of the port next season any grain moving for export through Churchill this fall will have certain advantages, as no elevator or storage charges, port charges, or pilotage fees will be exacted. Partly due to this it appears probable, from investigations by the department, that grain may be shipped via Hudson bay this season, notwithstanding relatively high insurance rates, as cheaply as it can be shipped to Europe through present recognized channels. On this basis, the department has endeavoured to interest the western grain trade in the proposed movement, so far without success, due probably to the demoralized state of the grain trade owing to world conditions.
The position of the matter at present, therefore, is this: the government has fulfilled the implied obligation of its predecessors and will have the terminal facilities at Churchill available on September 15 as planned. The railway, the dock, the elevator, and the necessary aids to navigation have been provided. Vessels will not proceed to Churchill to load unless grain is sold abroad for delivery via that port. The matter is thus in the hands of the grain exporters. It is no part of the business of the government to undertake the purchase and sale of grain for movement via Churchill, any more than for movement via any other Canadian port. If the test movement is to take place, the responsibility is therefore on the grain dealers of western Canada. The facilities will be available and if the grain interests are not in a position to take advantage of the opportunity to give them a practical test after September 15, it will be necessary to postpone the handling of grain through Churchill until the formal completion of work next year.

I want to thank the finance minister for producing those figures for me. I did not expect to get them so quickly, Mr. Chairman, and so in the meantime I did some figuring myself, and I do not think that my figures are very far out.
The finance minister informed the committee last night that the total amount of anthracite coal imported into this Dominion last year from the United States was 2,748,000 tons approximately. In order to arrive at some conclusion as to the amount that would go into the province of Ontario, and that is what I am more vitally interested in, I figured that 70 per cent of the total importations of anthracite coal from the United States last year found a market in the province of Ontario, and from the figures just given by the Minister of Finance I do not think I am very far out. Seventy per cent of 2,748,000 tons gives us the amount approximately of 1,950,000 tons of American anthracite which found a market in Ontario last year. If I am very far out one way or the other I hope the Minister of Finance will correct me, but I believe those figures are approximately correct. Now the duty of 40 cents a ton on the importation of 2,748,000 tons last year would bring in a revenue of SI,-
100,000	approximately, and taking 70 per cent of that we find that the people of the province of Ontario will have to pay in duty on coal, based on last year's importation, approximately $790,000. Again, if I am wrong in these figures, I hope the Minister of Finance will correct me.

speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman would be wrong, would he not? Forty cents on 1,973,000 tons would hardly give the figure he mentioned, and 70 per cent of that would give a much lesser sum than he mentioned.

For the sake of
argument I think I would be safe in calling

it three-quarters of a million dollars, $750,000. I do not think that would be very far out. In the province of Ontario and especially in the western part of the province, the fuel question is a very vital one. We are absolutely dependent upon fuel that has to be transported a long way to reach our market, and the supply from the United States, whether we like it or not, is the nearest to the market, and consequently transportation charges on American anthracite coming into Ontario are less than the transportation charges would be on coal from either eastern Canada or western Canada. As to the quality of the coal, I shall have something to say in a few minutes. So far as assistance to the coal industry is concerned, both in the eastern part of Canada and in the west, I think I am voicing the almost unanimous opinion of the people of western Ontario when I say that they are perfectly willing in any way possible to assist the coal industry in both the east and the west of this country. I find no fault with subsidies or bonuses or subventions or other assistance that can be given to the coal industry of both eastern and western Canada, but when, on top of such assistance, you impose a duty of 40 cents a ton on anthracite coal, which burden is borne largely by the people of the province of Ontario, as the figures I have given show, it is piling on generosity a little too much.
I have not yet heard any explanation from the Minister of Finance why he imposed this 40 cents a ton duty. The finance minister has been very candid and frank in his explanations on all the other tariff items. Some of them I did not agree with, but I give the Minister of Finance credit for candour and frankness. To the best of my recollection he has not touched on this duty on anthracite coal. Although last night he did deliver a very instructive address to the committee on the coal industry, I do not think he referred to anthracite coal at all, and I should be very glad if, when I finish my remarks, he would give an explanation of just what reason he had for imposing this duty. He has already told the committee on several occasions of being interviewed by different people who. were asking for tariff increases on different commodities. He told the committee, for instance, about the interview' he had with an American citizen with regard to the silk industry. He also told the committee about an interview that he had with a gentleman from Montreal with regard to the safety pin industry, and with respect to those duties he was quite frank and gave the reasons for

The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Rhodes) in his remarks last night referred, of course, to the coal industry in his own province, as did also the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. MacDonald), and I find no fault with them at all in doing everything they can within reason to stimulate and develop the coal industry in their province. But the Minister of Fisheries said: "The people of Ontario can burn coke." In that he is not correct.
He is absolutely correct.
Do you live in Ontario?
No, in Nova Scotia.

In Halifax. I am
afraid my hon. friend from Halifax is somewhat prejudiced in his views.

Not a bit. I know what I
am talking about, that is all.

We use the same kind of
furnace as you do in Ontario.

I use a Hamilton-made

And so could you in Ontario.

What part of Ontario is the

Not your part.
I live in western Ontario.
If there is one member I would not attempt to speak for-God forbid!-it is the hon. member for South Essex.
Because you got enough when you came to South Essex; that is why.

Getting back to the coal situation in the province of Ontario I wish to say to the Minister of Fisheries that there are some furnaces in that province in which coke cannot be burned; as a matter of fact there are very few places in that province where it can be burned. I should like to point out that in thousands and thousands,-yes, tens of thousands-of the homes in the province of Ontario, and
especially in western Ontario, there are no furnaces. In those homes they use the old fashioned coal stove which will not with any degree of satisfaction burn coke.
Has the hon. member ever tried it?
Yes, I have tried it.
The hon. member has had experience?
I know whereof I speak.
Apparently the education of the hon. member has been neglected.
Mr. Chairman, are you going to attempt to keep order in this committee.
Order.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I should like to say to the Minister of Fisheries that in most but not all of the furnaces in the province of Ontario one may burn a mixture of coke and anthracite coal. In very few that I have seen however can coke be burned alone. Going back to the question of stoves I will admit that one could burn in them a mixture of anthracite coal and coke. It is not always convenient however for people to do that. The natural fuel for the people of western Ontario, I am sorry to admit, is the anthracite from the United States. Last night the Minister of Fisheries stated that in thirty-five years the coal fields in the United States would be depleted.
Twenty-five years.

I understood the
minister to say thirty-five.
I wish to correct my hon. friend. I read from a statement published in the year 1921.

I understood the minister to say thirty-five; I am sorry if I am misquoting him. I do not know however that hon. members of the committee are particularly concerned whether in twenty-five or thirty-five year's the coal in the United States will be depleted. I think that is a matter for the consideration of governments following the present one-because I do not expect this government will be in power twenty-five or thirty-five years from now.

I think the hon. member has another guess coming.

Owing to the advance in scientific methods and other like considerations I think the whole of the Dominion of Canada will be relieved from the necessity of using coal as a fuel. In the meantime however whether we like it or not we are dependent upon United States anthracite coal for fuel purposes. If it were pointed out to me that the imposition of this tariff of 40 cents per ton is for revenue purposes I do not know that I would raise any serious objection. So far however the Prime Minister has made no announcement whatever, and I wish to say to him that the proposed duty will not help the coal industry either in the east or in the west. As I understand it the coal in Nova Scotia is not adapted to the heating of houses as is the American anthracite coal. Then there is the further point of higher transportation charges. For years and years, even going back twelve or fifteen years, there have been commissions and committees which have investigated the matter of bringing Alberta coal to the province of Ontario. Trial shipments have been made, but the whole scheme has been abandoned for several reasons, one being the long haulage and transportation charges. A more vital reason however was that Alberta coal is not adapted to domestic uses. Had the people of the province of Ontario for purely patriotic reasons been able to burn Alberta coal they would have been glad to substitute it for the American product. That cannot be done however, and for that reason I say that in the present instance a duty or tax is being imposed on the people of the province of Ontario,-and why? I should be pleased to have the reason from the Prime Minister. He may be able to convince me that there is a reason, and if he succeeds I shall be very glad to tell him that I am convinced. At the moment however I protest vigorously not on behalf of my hon. friend from South Essex (Mr. Gott) but on behalf of the people of South Perth whom I represent and who are opposed to the imposition of the duty of 40 cents a ton on anthracite coal.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for South Perth (Mr. Sanderson) has been engaged in addressing the committee in his usual insipid manner.
Order.

He has proven conclusively
that he knows nothing at all about coal.

Well, we will hear
something now.

He has proven' he is not a
dealer in coal, and has also proven that he is not a dealer in common, decent every-day ethics or in political decency. The hon. member came into my riding, and I was pleased to see him there. I should like however to have just a few moments to discuss his manner when in that riding.
Knowing that the hon. member for South Perth would speak to-day and knowing that he always exaggerates his statements, last night I wired Mr. F. M. Falls at Amherst-burg, Ontario, as follows:
Informed that the new duties on coal were conducive to you obtaining Detroit prices. Please wire me day letter early Thursday.
To-day I received from him the following: wire:
Answering your wire. Detroit coke producers charged us 50 cents over Detroit price but reduced their prices to us from five ninety to five dollars when new duty added.
That wire is from a person who knows something about the coal business. Practically every furnace in western Ontario is built to use coke. The duty means a reduction of 90 cents a ton on coke used by the people of western Ontario.

Does my hon. friend state
that Detroit dealers in coke or producers of coke have reduced the price 90 cents a ton to Canadians; is that right?
Shall I read it again?

I wish to be clear; is that
the statement made by the hon. member?

That is the statement which
came to me from F. W. Falls, a dealer in Amherstburg, Ontario.
That there is a reduction of 90 cents a ton on coke?
Yes.
What about the $1 that the government is setting up against American coke; does that not wipe out the advantage?

It is being absorbed by
the American dealers.

I do not wish to delay the
committee, and I am not going to-

Does the hon. member wish
me to read the telegrams again?

No. Speaking last night 1
desired to learn from the Minister of Finance, if possible, just how the 40 cent duty on anthracite coal fitted in with his all-Canadian fuel policy. The Minister of Fisheries replied, but in all courtesy I am bound to say his

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
explanation was not convincing. I should like to have from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett) some substantial reason why the people of Ontario and of parts of Quebec will undoubtedly have to pay more for their anthracite coal than would be the case if the duty had not been applied. I said last night also, that if by reason of placing this duty on anthracite coal you can promote the coal industry in any other part of Canada, then there is an argument in its favour. The Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Rhodes) has not said so. He did say that he thought it would promote the use of coke in Ontario, and that the people of Ontario and elsewhere by using coke would save, I think he said, $2.34 a ton. The proof of the pudding is in the eating. I know very well that a good many people in my own city and district and in western Ontario generally are already using coke; they have done so ever since anthracite coal went sky high during the war when its quality was so bad that we could hardly use it; some of them have continued to use coke, and occasionally others are using it. But I submit that the people of my riding in particular are pretty thrifty folks and they are not going to pay $234 more per ton for a commodity if they can get a cheaper substitute. Yet the greater proportion of them still use hard coal and I think they will continue to do so.
Then my hon. friend the Minister of Fisheries, proceeded, I think, to destroy his own argument, and some information came out from the Minister of Finance which had the same effect. The Minister of Fisheries said the people of Ontario should use coke as the people do in the maritime provinces. Am I right?

My hon. friend is quite
wrong. I did not make any comparison of the use of coke in the maritime provinces as a matter of quantity. I merely referred to its use there to illustrate that it could be used as a substitute for anthracite coal, that as a matter of science it was possible to do so.
Then my hon. friend's argument is that the people of Nova Scotia are using coke and now he is recommending that the people of Ontario do the same.

They are using soft coal
largely.

His statement is rather contradicted by the Minister of Finance, who said that last year the province of Nova Scotia imported from Great Britain, the United States and Russia about 80,000 tons of anthracite coal. They are using it themselves.

It simply means that that coal was imported through Nova Scotian ports; it by no means follows that the coal was used in the province of Nova Scotia. It is true some of it was, but no doubt the bulk of it was transported by rail into other provinces.

We will let that go. But
the argument is very largely destroyed in this way. I take it that if we are to be discouraged in the use of anthracite coal in Ontario and Quebec, it is at least with this partial purpose in view-apart from revenue, perhaps-that coal from the maritimes shall be imported either in the form of coke produced there or to be converted into coke in Ontario.
Not necessarily. Why not give employment to the people who are producing the coke, even if it is produced from American soft coal.

But that does not touch
the question of a national fuel policy. That deals with unemployment-an entirely different matter.
Yes.

If it is the intention to develop a national fuel policy, and by discouraging the people of Ontario and Quebec in the use of American anthracite lead to the use of Nova Scotia soft coal in the form of coke produced there or in the form of coke produced in Ontario from Nova Scotia coal, then why does he say, as he did last night, that so far as the people of Ontario are concerned they need not use Nova Scotia coal at all, they can still bring in soft coal from the United States and get a drawback on the duty they pay on it? That merely means you are going to develop the soft coal fields of the United States, if you like, but it has not anything to do with developing a national fuel policy, and I think my hon. friend will admit this if he looks at it from that point of view. That does not help the Nova Scotia coal industry. And I am sure every member of the house, including those who come from Alberta, will admit that it has been absolutely proven to be impracticable to transport Alberta coal to the province of Ontario, to say nothing of the province of Quebec. I wish the Minister of Finance would give a reasonable explanation of how this policy of placing a duty on hard coal, which is not produced in Canada at all, fits in with the development of a national fuel policy. If there are no better arguments to be advanced than have been advanced so far,

I submit the whole effect of the policy will be that the people of my province and the people of Quebec will be obliged to pay higher prices for their hard coal at a time when they can little afford to do so. If it is a matter of revenue, I say again, as I said yesterday, that that revenue might very well be raised in some other way.
May I inform my hon. friend that negotiations are under way at the present time for the establishment of two coke plants in western Ontario.

I should like to ask the Minister of Finance this-and in what I am about to say there is a criticism of the action of the former government of which I was a member-an action to which I was never a consenting party, if I may say so, as my hon. friend the former Minister otf the Interior (Mr. Stewart) knows. I stated last night that there was discrimination in the production of coke in Ontario. My hon. friend from South Essex (Mr. Gott) said a moment ago that there is in contemplation the establishment of two more coke ovens in western Ontario. If the producers use a certain process, as I suppose they will, they will get a drawback of 99 per cent of the duty which they pay on American coal. Am I right in that assumption? But as I pointed out last night, there is discrimination in Ontario. For instance, there is a coke oven of the kind at Hamilton, and I think there is another at Montreal. And by the way, I think when the Montreal people received the privilege of the drawback it was never really intended that they should continue to use American soft coal; it was intended that they should1 use Nova Scotia coal. But they are still using American coal and getting the drawback of the duty they pay on that coal, and thus it is working against the interests of the Nova Scotia coal producers. But the matter I wish to come to is this. The coke producers at Hamilton receive the drawback of the duty paid on the soft coal from which their coke is produced. We have in western Ontario a considerable number of municipalities that own their gas plants as well as several other public utilities. That is true of my home city of Kitchener. They produce a very good quality of coke as a by-product of their gas. They import the soft coal from the United States in order to produce their gas and coke, but they get no drawback as do their competitors in the city of Hamilton. I submit that that injustice ought to be remedied, either by way of refusing the drawback to the Hamilton people-and I have no desire to offend my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Bell) nor of saying anything that might in-
jure a legitimate industry, or, what would be fairer, by extending the same privilege of the drawback to the municipalities of Ontario that are using American coal in the production of coke.

I have no intention of entering into the dispute with regard to the relative fuel merits of coke and anthracite coal. The statement has been made that the domestic coal of Alberta cannot be transported economically to Ontario. I cannot allow that statement to go uncontradieted. Of course, that coal could not be brought here economically when the rates were up to $8 or $10 a ton; but now we have practically an assured rate of $6.75 a ton, and Alberta domestic coal can be sold on the markets of Ontario to provide a substantial portion of the fuel requirements of the people of this province.
That is not anthracite coal.

No, but it is a lot better than any anthracite coal that comes into Ontario. It has been abundantly proved that it gives far better results. It gives more for the money than any other coal that can be burned.
More than coke?

It is better than coke,
but I am not going to enter into that dispute; hon. members can fight it out among themselves. The domestic coal of Alberta is superior to coke or to the anthracite coal that comes from the United States. This has been proved by test shipments which were brought down here by the government some years ago, when 33,000 tons were placed in the homes of Ontario. That supply gave splendid results. There has been no difficulty because of any complaint about the quality of the coal, nor was there the slightest objection on the part of the people of Ontario to the use of that coal; for in fact those who received it were highly gratified with the results and were extremely anxious to have further supplies. The difficulty was that there was no stability in the market; the $6.75 rate per ton was not fixed; it was only spasmodic. But recently this rate-I am not going into any details-has been established on a more permanent basis; and with a permanent rate of $6.75 we can secure a stable market. With such a market the dealers here would take Alberta coal and dispose of it to Ontario householders.
The difficulty in the past has been this. When the coal was shipped here and marketed the householder, having used it, was so sati3-field with the results that later on he tried to

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
get further supplies of Alberta coal. But he found that the dealer did not have it; he could not bring it in on account of the freight rates, which had gone up in the meantime. Once a permanent rate is fixed and stability established in handling the coal shipped to the dealers, the dealers will keep supplies of it; and we have every hope that, under these circumstances, Alberta domestic coal will take its place in the markets of Ontario. Let me repeat that it gives better results, as has been proved. The experiments carried out by the Ontario government and the Dominion Fuel Board have shown this.
The rate has now been fixed at $6.75 per ton until March 31 next, and I may say to the house and to the administration that in the meantime we intend to do everything humanly possibly to bring pressure to bear upon the government with a view to having that rate made a fixture for all time to come, as a maximum at any rate. In that event the dealers in Ontario, through such means as will be taken by the Alberta operators, by the government of that province and otherwise, will keep permanent supplies so that they may be able to meet the demands of regular customers.
I should like the hon. member for North W aterloo (Mr. Euler) to pass the news on to the many citizens of his excellent constituency and particularly to the people in the manufacturing city of Kitchener. I hope he will inform them that there is no fuel on the continent equal to Alberta coal. Those of us who have lived in Ontario where we burned American anthracite, and who have since been burning Alberta coal, know the difference. There is no comparison between Alberta domestic coal and other supplies; and, as I have said, we get better results.
Perhaps I might refer to the situation in Winnipeg. I have confidence in the use of tariffs; I have confidence in the dumping clause, and so on. They serve their purpose. But at the same time I submit that in Ontario, and in other parts of Canada, there must be a spirit of loyalty and a-desire to help the producers of this country, wherever they may operate, to sell their commodities to the consuming public. In Winnipeg there is a large public utility in the central heating plant, and recently that concern purchased 43,000 tons of coal from the United States. I am subject to correction, but I believe that this coal was brought in a considerable time ago; and those who are interested in these plants in Winnipeg- they are American interests-gave the Alberta operators to understand that they proposed
to purchase bituminous coal for their purposes. When the time came for their purchase, without giving the Alberta operators an opportunity to tender, they placed their orders with their friends in Virginia. Now, they made no money; they saved nothing; and they did not get as good coal as the Alberta operators could have given them. All they did was to assist some American friends in Virginia. And while they helped their American friends to the extent of 43,000 tons, they withdrew that much business from the coal mines of southern Alberta, at a time when the miners of that district are very much in need of employment in face of the coming winter.

I wish
to refer to a statement made by the Prime Minister last night with regard to the Saskatchewan coal field. I fear it is misleading, although I do not suggest that he made it intentionally. The fact is, however, that those who do not understand the situation will probably be misled by that statement. It appears at page 3817 of Hansard:
In Saskatchewan and Manitoba there is a further deposit of lignite coal. Scientists tell us that the quality of that coal is not as high as that of the lignite coal to which I have previously referred. It is now being briquetted. During the war and after we spent a substantial sum of money in experiments, in this connection, as a result of which, supplemented by more recent scientific knowledge, that area or measure of coal has been developed by the production of briquettes and a substantial market has been created in the city of Winnipeg and elsewhere in the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan for the products of those mines.
From that statement, those who do not understand the conditions might think that the only -market we find for that lignite coal of southern Saskatchewan is the demand for the briquetted product. There is quite an extensive market in Winnipeg for the raw lignite, and that which is processed by briquetting is only a very small proportion of the coal mined in that area.

It is a friable coal and briquetting was resorted to in order to enable it to be carried considerable distances.

I understand that. But we have found a steady improvement in that coal, so that it is possible to market it now without fear of any appre-

ciable disintegration as suggested by the Prime Minister. Moreover, as I said last night, even though it does disintegrate there is a mechanical device, now used extensively in furnaces, which creates a greater draft, with the result that this coal can be burned much more satisfactorily than before.
Does the one-seventh of a cent per ton per mile mentioned in the budget speech apply to briquettes as well as to the raw coal?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Some question has been raised with respect to this, and the matter is now in the hands of the Minister of Mines. I think it was intended that this subvention should apply to all the products of these mines, but the matter is being investigated by the fuel board and action will be taken at an early date.

I believe the one-seventh of a cent per mile will give some assistance in the case of briquettes, but I would again draw the attention of the Prime Minister to the fact that when the subventions of last year were put into force, a subvention of SO cents was given to the Saskatchewan lignite coal in the Manitoba market. One-seventh of a cent per mile on 280 miles would mean approximately 40 cents, a reduction of ten cents. My information is that the subvention allowed on Alberta coal will increase the old subvention by from 12 to 14 cents, which means that the Saskatchewan fields are being discriminated against to the extent of some 22 or 24 cents per ton. This is rather unfair and it will mean that the miners of southern Saskatchewan will not be able to hold the market which they have gained in Winnipeg. I hope the Prime Minister will take into serious consideration the suggestion I made last night when I said that I thought it would be nothing more than fair, considering the quality of coal produced, that the same subvention be given to Saskatchewan as is given to Nova Scotia. This amounts to one-fifth of a cent per mile which would mean approximately 56 cents instead of 40 cents to the Winnipeg market. This would be no more than justice to the coal miners of southern Saskatchewan.

Mr. Chairman, I notice the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) has retired and is now carbonizing tobacco by induced draft in back behind the curtains. I presume the hon. member knows that gas coke is a by-product fuel of relatively low heating value.
I will not admit that.

This fuel runs about one hundred cubic feet to the ton. By-product coke runs from 45 to 50 cubic feet to the ton, anthracite from 30 to 35 and bituminous coal about 40 cubic feet. The value of these fuels can be estimated roughly from the cubical contents. Coke can be burned in any stove in which bituminous or anthracite coal can be burned.
No, it cannot.
I say it can.
We say no.
The hon. member does not know.
The hon. member burns only wood.
All that is required to burn coke in any stove which will burn any other kind of fuel is a sufficient supply of oxygen.
May I ask-

I did not interrupt the
hon. member and he should wait until I have finished. If he has any question to ask at that time, I will answer it, but in the meantime I intend to proceed with my lecture. The best anthracite coal from the United States does not run over 88 to 98 per cent fixed carbon. The coke manufactured in Nova Scotia, and I presume it is made equally as well in Hamilton, will run from 92 to 93 per cent in fixed carbon, and the fuel value is determined by the amount of carbon. The secret of burning coke, as in burning other forms of fuel, is to provide sufficient oxygen to burn the fixed carbon; the higher the percentage of fixed carbon, the more oxygen required to burn it. If this fuel is dealt with intelligently there will be no difficulty. I will admit that there is a little technique in addition to providing a sufficient supply of air, or oxygen; if it is continuously stirred up there will be difficulty; all that is required is to put fresh coke on top, keeping a relatively deep incandescent fuel body, withdraw what little ash or clinker there may be in the bottom, and supply sufficient oxygen. That is the whole story.

Mr. Chairman, while
this item was being discussed last night, I laid before the committee as briefly as possible the situation obtaining in certain coal areas in the province of Alberta which supply steam coal to the Canadian railways. I asked at that time that some consideration be given to these miners, not by way of tariff changes because that would raise unfairly the price

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
of coal to the railways who are forced to buy as cheaply as possible; not by way of freight subvention because this coal is used by the railways themselves and a subvention would be of no value, but rather by way of some form of bonus to equalize the difference in cost between Canadian and American coal.
The greatest handicap facing the miners of steam coal in this particular area, as well as in others, is the fact that coal is brought in from the United States at a slightly lower cost. When the Prime Minister was speaking, I had hoped that he would have made some reference to the matter and indicated that at least serious consideration would be given to this situation. I may offend the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) by saying that I am subject to corruption, although I would not go as far as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) and say that I was willing to wallow in iniquity to secure some assistance for the people in my riding, but there are times when one's convictions as to what is economically sound must be put aside, especially when facing certain facts. The facts in this case are that many of these people are out of work, and those who are working are working only part time and are not in receipt of sufficient wages to keep themselves and their families in decency. The little town of Nordegg, situated in the Brazeau coal district, is isolated from all other parts of the country. This is a country town which has no source of income save from the mines. When these mines are not working to capacity, the men suffer most severely.
It is not often that I bring up events which happened during the last elections, because such a course is not often relevant to the discussion nor is it of much value, but I would suggest that because of the very definite promises made, not by the Prime Minister, but on his behalf during the last election, I lost about four-fifths of the votes in that area. The miners were convinced that if the Conservative party was returned to power they would receive such assistance as would enable them to carry on. While it is true that these men voted against me, none the less, having been elected, my duty is to see that they should receive such consideration as will enable them to carry on and survive in this struggle for existence.

I did not understand
the subvention to apply to the railway and therefore I suggested that to take the place of that subvention a bonus should be paid- not sufficient to enable them to use coal throughout the whole area, because that would be economically unsound, but at least sufficient to extend the area eastward within which Alberta coal could be used, and before it came into competition with United States coal which takes its place I think a little bit west of Winnipeg; it is a varying point. It is a matter of policy, of administration, as to the extent of the bonus, as to the distance east to which this coal can be carried. But I believe a comparatively small amount would make up the difference between the cost of the two coals, particularly as I am not pleading for collieries which are working under any handicap as to cheap and economic production. Those mines are being operated

very economically; the nature of the mines has provided that the coal itself is cheap, so that this is not a matter of bonusing a system that is economically unsound. There is no submarine mining there, no natural causes which would militate against the use of that coal. I should like to get some assurance in this regard.

Whereas, the unfortunate position in which employees of the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation find themselves has been brought to the attention of the provincial and federal governments on different occasions; particularly the serious situation of the nail and wire mill, which has been practically closed down for the past six months, and the yard department, getting from one to two days' work each week; and the workers of the city suffering in general;

February 11, 1931. That was the situation in Sydney, and that is the resolution that was passed. We have had since then three changes in connection with the coal policy, culminating in the policy now before us. We had a temporary sort of fixation of prices for duty purposes on slack and run of mine, $1 and $155. That was reduced, and then this policy was brought down. Now I understand that the value which has been fixed on slack and run of mine for duty purposes is being taken off altogether. I want to ask the Prime Minister what he thinks the result would have been if at that time he had said at Sydney: I can only give you 25 cents on bituminous coal and restore the duty on anthracite to the extent of 40 cents, and I presume the American dealers will reduce their prices in order to meet that duty, and on coke I will put back the one dollar per ton that we took off the duty years ago, and I will do a little better in the matter of subventions- what does he think would have been the response?
What did he do? He did this: Under the former government the subventions on all-rail coal coming to Ontario and Quebec were figured in this way: the government undertook to pay all the freight on coal above three dollars. That meant that in some cases the bonus contributed by the government went as high as $3.70. What has my right hon. friend done? He has said that the maximum amount which shall be contributed in connection with all-rail coal shall be $2. He has taken off the maximum in that respect and made the contribution less. He has increased the maximum on one item. He has added 75 cents to the maximum on coal, water-hauled to Montreal and forwarded by rail to Ontario. In other words, he has taken off the bonus with one hand, and he is paying it out with the other. If he had proposed that policy at Inverness and Sydney, does he think that

Replying to the
minister who has just taken his seat, I should say that the fuel policy of the present government consists largely in following in the footsteps of their predecessors. Certainly so far as subventions are concerned that is the case. I understand the policy of the present government is intended to go a little farther than that of the late government. That seems to be the contention so far as the maritime provinces are concerned, and I shall not discuss that point further. So far as Saskatchewan is concerned, however, the conditions will be worse. How can I go back to Saskatchewan and extol the national fuel policy when, so far as Saskatchewan is concerned, the subventions are not as satisfactory as they were under the former government? As I understood the Minister of Mines (Mr. Gordon) last night, the matter is still under consideration, and I believe the Prime Minister expressed himself in similar terms. I hope they will take the matter into serious consideration because in that province there is good lignite coal of a much better quality than that which the farmers travelled thirty or forty miles to get. At that time they were getting only the out-cropping of comparatively low grade lignite, but now when 
they are down several hundred feet they are getting good quality coal. In spite of the fact that it has a high water content and in spite of the small subvention it has been forcing itself on the markets in competition with other coals. Unless he has very good cause, I hope the Prime Minister will not discriminate against Saskatchewan coal. If he has any reasons to submit to the committee as to why he even proposes a lower rate in Saskatchewan as compared with that in Alberta, I should like to hear them.

are some observations I should like to make concerning the remarks of my hon. friend from Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston).

Let me tell the committee about the conditions that existed in Sydney at the time the resolution was passed and

the interview was given by Dr. Black. The people in Sydney, like the people in many other parts of Canada, are too fond of running to the government to do anything; they ask the government to do this and to do that. In the city of Sydney we took another course altogether. We appointed a community committee to handle the unemployment relief, and that committee headed by Dr. Black- a very patriotic spirited gentleman indeed- undertook the collection of clothing, food and cash. Not one dollar was obtained from the municipality, nor from this government, nor from the provincial government. That shows what can be done by a proper community spirit. All we want in this country is that that spirit shall prevail in every community. We do not want these demoralizing cries of, 'What are you going to do about unemployment"? 'When are you going to bring down your unemployment policy"? Our friends opposite are glorifying themselves by emphasizing the distress through which we are passing to-day, and they are trying to make political capital out of the poverty that unfortunately exists in certain districts.

I have listened patiently to
the debate and I think there are one or two points in connection with it which should be brought to the attention of the government. The case for the bituminous coal operators in Alberta has been very well placed before the committee by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), and I will not go further into it. 1 would impress upon the Prime Minister that in order to give the bituminous coal mining industry of Alberta a fair chance to secure the Manitoba market, some reduction should be made in the freight rates between the mountain division and Winnipeg. The freight rate from Blairmore to Winnipeg, 846 miles, is S5.10, while from Sydney to Montreal, 980 miles, it is $4.50 a ton. If the rate from the mountains to Winnipeg were on a comparative mileage basis with the rate between Sydney and Montreal, the bituminous coal operators would not have very much trouble getting their coal into the Winnipeg market.
I was glad to hear what the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Rhodes) said in regard to the national fuel policy of the government. I have no criticism to make of what they have
done so far. I did not expect the Prime Minister would be able to fulfil some of the promises made by certain of his supporters in the campaign because in my constituency my opponent used this placard:
Vote for J. D. Matheson and steady work for Canadian miners. The fuel policy of the Conservative party will accomplish this.
Of course, I told the miners at the time that the Conservative party could not at this stage bring down a fuel policy which would give all of them steady work. I still feel I was right in making that statement.
I desire to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister the unfortunate conditions which are confronting the miners in my district. In 1929 the Bellevue mine worked 172 days, and some of the other mines for a slightly longer period. An outside man drawing $4.40 a day would earn that year $750. In 1930 I think the mine worked 126 days, and at the same rate of pay that man would earn S504. Some of the men have large families, and I am sure that members of the committee will agree that no man could maintain a family on such small earnings. Last winter when I was in Blairmore I secured a statement of the wages earned by about twenty of the miners for the previous month, and I find the average is $29.82. One man with eight children earned $29.10; another with nine children earned S27.50. That will give hon. members some indication of the very small wages with which these miners have been trying to carry on. Some of them have been out of work altogether and have been granted relief. I have before me a statement, signed by the mayor of the town of Blairmore, in regard to some of the men who were getting relief work. One of them with a family of five or six children had a balance due him from the Home bank of $1,513; another one with six children had a balance of $643 due him from the Home bank; another one with six children had a balance of $937 due him from the Home bank. I mention these bank balances to show that some of these men are of a very thrifty type. But no matter how thrifty they may have been, the lean years have wiped out any savings they had, even though they were fortunate enough to deposit them in some other bank. I bring this to the attention of the government in the hope that they will be prepared to give some direct relief unless more work is provided for the miners; and I do not think it will be possible to provide sufficient work in the mines to enable those men to make a livelihood. Just a week ago

The mine here is still working very poor- we only worked fourteen days in May and eleven days in June with 100 of the crew not working.

The best method of encouraging production of more farm products in western Canada would be to adopt the amendment to the budget moved from this comer of the house. A suspension of the redemption of our notes in gold at this time would, I am sure, bring about a depreciation of our currency, which would put us on a basis where we could fairly compete with Australia and the Argentine; this in turn would encourage further production an our farms. That is the only way of dealing with the deplorable situation which faces us in western Canada, particularly in the mining area. The wheat crop this year is estimated to be about half that of last year, so we can look for comparatively little employment in the mining areas this winter. I desire to give the government credit for the efforts they have made to improve conditions in the coal industry, but at the same time I want to point out that it will be absolutely necessary that some unemployment relief be provided for that area this winter.

Just a word, Mr. Chairman, in reply to my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. MacDonald). I listened with interest to his lecture on non-partisanship. It is really a new doctrine to come from him, but we accept lectures of that kind whatever their source may be. It is not so long since the hon. gentleman went about his constituenc}r with a lump of Russian coal in his pocket, exhibiting it to the meetings there and telling everybody that these horrid Grits were destroying the coal industry of Cape Breton by permitting something like 100,000 tons of Russian coal to come in annually. And that representation I will not designate as mean partisanship-that, I believe, was the expression he used-but I will be charit-

able and call it enthusiastic party loyalty. I find no fault with him if he thinks it good politics to do that. But at the same time he must not lecture others on partisanship. We find, in fact, that the 100,000 tons of Russian anthracite coal, which did not compete with Canadian coal, has been embargoed by the government, but that 156,000,000 worth of American will still come in. Yet my hon. friend, in that spirit of non-partisanship of which we have had evidence, accepts that situation. In other words, he strains at a gnat and swallows a camel.
Hoof and all.

Another instance of his
non-partisanship appeared in the fact that the other night he refrained from taking part in a debate when my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre suggested that tariffs on certain articles might be accompanied by a condition as to hours of labour and rates of wages. It was only last year that my hon. friend, when he was on this side of the house, in that spirit of non-partisanship which always actuates him, stood up and proposed to the then government a resolution that this should be done. It was due to the steel workers, he said.

I was
not in favour of that; I do not think it is possible. I should be only too strongly in favour of it if it were possible, but I do not see how you can couple such a condition with the tariff.

My hon. friend has seen
the light; since he has moved across to the other side he realizes the impossibility of it. That is the spirit of non-partisanship that moves him.
Now, Mr. Chairman^ I suggest that it might be just as well for the hon. gentleman not to lecture other people about running down the country, implying that they glory in misery, and so on. I put on Hansard the other night a few statements made by the Prime Minister during his election campaign last year, and if anyone wishes to take the trouble to read those statements he can judge for himself whether or not what the Prime Minister described as the country's extremity was being exploited by him for political purposes. Let us give the right hon. gentleman credit for the highest motives; but do not let us have any lectures to other people when they happen to bring to the attention of the house conditions as they exist. Does not my hon. friend from South Cape Breton think that when the Prime Minister made a declaration about the cry of women and children being heard across the country-women and children

calling upon us to ease their pain-he was rather encroaching upon the preserves which the hon. gentleman now regards as inviolable in debate? I give all credit to the community effort down there to meet the situation. But I repeat that there is a great difference between the promise given the people of Nova Scotia with regard to a national fuel policy and this first step, to use the words of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Rhodes), towards the fulfilment of that undertaking. speechtext:

These issues were raised differently by other speakers as well. My hon. friend from North Waterloo has been answered by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). One of these hon. gentlemen says that the result of this anthracite tariff will be to increase the price in Ontario, and the hon. member for South Perth says the same thing. The answer given by the hon. member for Shclburne-Yarmouth is that the American producer will absorb the 40 cents.
What is your answer?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman from North Waterloo pointed out that in cabinet he had had occasion to differ from his colleagues, and he called upon one of his former colleagues to witness to that statement. Whether or not it is intended this afternoon that we
shall have an entire repudiation of doctrines which the hon. gentleman formerly held, I know not. But we have had a striking example of what one might call the remnants of a left-over administration. I have never in my lifetime listened to such severe condemnation of the policies of a government of which an hon. gentleman was a member. I have never heard so severe a condemnation as that which he made this afternoon, ant my only wonder is that he did not resign from the administration which he so much opposed within and so violently supported without. At any rate, the answer given by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth is that the American producer will absorb the 40 cents for the purpose of retaining the market.
Now, there are three reasons for this tax.

The hard coal tax.
Mi-. BENNETT: The hard coal tax. First, it is part of a national endeavour to establish and maintain a fuel policy in Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The admitted coail resources of the country have been referred to this afternoon by many hon. gentlemen, particularly the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Stanley); and when I said last night that the prodution of coal had reached over 6,000.000 tons in Alberta. I but stated a fact which everyone knows. And the quality of that coal is such that I have no doubt it will one day be the fuel used in Ontario. The first reason for the tax is, therefore, the fact that we are endeavouring to establish and maintain that policy. And when I say we are endeavouring, I mean just what I said in Inverness. At that time I stated that if elected we would meet the situation. And we have met it. Whether we have met it successfully or not will be evident hereafter; but we did say that we would meet it, and at the first session of parliament we have done so.
The Minister of Fisheries says you have not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I did not intimate to the delegation what the policy of the government would be, for the simple and obvious reason that had I done so I should not have done my duty by parliament. For this was a matter with respect to which parliament had a right to be informed. It involved the revenues of the country; and, as I have been reminded so frequently by constitutionalists who are not lawyers, the duty of the government is to make these matters known to the house before they are disclosed to anyone else. I said, however, that I would take the

Whether or not it has been met successfully, time will tell; but at least we have met it, and we have not apologized for inaction, as for nine long years our predecessors had reason to do.
The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth always runs true to form; and, with eyes shut, if one did not recognize his voice one would still be able to identify him by his observations; for there is no one so querulous, and no one whose cynicism touching poverty and unemployment and this fuel question is so well known. This afternoon he is again running true to form. He quotes something from February to prove that what was done in June was not adequate. He said that the measure taken in June was not a fulfilment of the promise made in January to the delegation that came here. He quotes some resolutions, passing over others, content to leave by half truths the impression he always tries to leave with audiences whom he addressses. And the result of his campaign in Nova Scotia during the last election is fully understood by those who have listened to his speeches in this house.
The second reason is that we are endeavouring to do something to promote inter-empire trade. When I heard hon. gentleman opposite mentioning $28,000,000 and $50,000,000 and other sums as being the value of the coal imported from the United States, I can only say that they could not have been in the committee this afternoon when I gave the importations of anthracite from the United States for the twelve months ended March 31, 1931, as being $20,145,000. When it is stated that the province of Quebec will have to pay 40 cents more per ton, I would tell the committee that the 
duty upon Welsh anthracite is nil, and Quebec as well as Ontario will be able to purchase its requirements of United Kingdom coal free of duty. Last year the province of Quebec purchased from Great Britain 836,693 tons of anthracite coal. This year the encouragement to buy this coal will be still greater, and we are certain that over one million tons of coal will be purchased from Great Britain to supply the anthracite requirements of this Dominion.
Last evening the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) indicated a further benefit which would be derived. He mentioned the direct benefit which would accrue to every member of the rural constituencies in western Canada, namely, the reduction of the rate in the handling of grain brought about by' the bringing of coal to this country. Instead, of vessels being forced to come to Montreal empty in order to obtain a return cargo of grain, they will now have cargoes of anthracite coal which will ensure a lower freight rate on grain than has prevailed heretofore. Is not that worth while?
There is a third reason, the encouraging of the production of coke in this country. Right here, let me ask the hon. memlber for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart): when the coke plant on the canal at Montreal was given assistance by his government, why was it permitted to be placed where a ship laden with Nova Scotia coal could not unload its cargo? Why was it, instead of giving some assistance and support to Canadian coal, this LaSalle plant was located so that only American coal could be used? Why, under these circumstances, was a bonus paid to this coke plant? These questions are being asked by everyone, but no answer has been given.
Cannot one ship go into the same place as another?

speechtext:
That is a matter for consideration. It may well be that as the people of Ontario become more fully accustomed to these fuels-the hon. gentleman has said that they are willing and ready to bear their part of the burden in every national purpose, and I believe that is true-then the situation alluded to may well take place. What I said last night, I repeat. If the scientific efforts now being made in laboratories result as I believe they will, in a complete revolution in the utilization of coal, I feel confident that an increasing quantity of Canadian coal will be used in the province of Ontario.
The hon. gentleman mentioned another reason, the necessity for revenue. In view of the subventions given to other parts of the country, this does provide some revenue. Just prior to June 1, a strong agitation was being carried on by representative citizens of the province of Nova Scotia. The contention was that all the benefits accruing from the tariff policy of this country were going to the people in upper Canada. It was contended that the people of Ontario and Quebec had no understanding or appreciation of their problems and had shown no willingness to help the province of Nova Scotia which consumed in such large quantities the manufactured products of the other provinces. The answer made was: has there ever been an appeal made to us when we have received protection for our industrial and manufacturing life and which involved our making a contribution for a national purpose or a national need, that we have not responded? The hon. member for North Waterloo has said that that is still the attitude of the people of Ontario, and I believe it is. Here is accorded one more opportunity with respect to revenue. Compensating adjustments are being made for the people of the lower provinces and far west who are large consumers of the products of central Canada, and the people of that section of the country are glad to avail themselves of the opportunity to advance the common interests of Canada as a whole.
These are the factors which have actuated this government in its effort to establish a national policy. I have never been blind to the difficulties which present themselves, and I have never indicated that I was blind to them. I said we would meet the situation. Do hon. members know of any government which has met its difficulties and the situations with which it was confronted during its life-time, as has this government during the last year?
We are making an effort to overcome the accumulated miseiy caused by the policies of preceding years. We have not dodged the issue.
There is no world depression now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

To hear hon. gentlemen talk, one would think that they and they alone knew what difficulties were. I know that there are those among them who say: How pleasant it is to think that the responsibility is not ours! That is their conception of their obligations. They were glad to be in power in the yearn of bounty and plenty; when there was no world depression they were willing to talk about their difficulties, but now that there is a world depression, they say: We are glad we are not over there. That is their idea of service to the commonwealth. They are glad to be in power in good times, and to be out in bad times. I said at Inverness, and I said last year, that if we came into power we would meet this difficulty. There is not an hon. member in this committee, or elsewhere, who can say that we have not met it. Whether or not we have met it successfully is a matter which time will tell.

speechtext:
I hesitate to rise after
listening to the lecture that has been delivered from the other side to members on this side of the house. I feel, however, I have a duty to perform, and notwithstanding the fear of receiving another of the lectures that have been so frequently given from the other side, I am going to venture into what is perhaps dangerous ground.	*
I notice an effort was made this afternoon to credit the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth with laying down the principle that the United States people would absorb the duty of 40 cents a ton on anthracite coal. Let me draw the attention of the committee to the record, so that we may have it clear. The Minister of Fisheries is the hon. gentleman who first propounded this principle. Speaking on the budget, he made this statement:
I submit that that tax, which was held up as a burden placed upon the people of Ontario and Quebec, need not be paid at all by the people of those provinces. In the first place, even if they buy anthracite coal, the treasury gets the benefit of the tax. It remains to be seen, however, how much of that tax will be paid by the producer. I venture to say, owing to the highly competitive nature of the business, that the larger portion, if not the whole of that tax, will be paid by the producer in the United States.
Now hon. members are attributing that to the hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth.
He said so.

He said so only in referring to what was said by the hon. member for South Essex, who stated this afternoon that the United States producer, in order to retain the market, would absorb the duty. The Minister of Fisheries agrees. I wish to ask him: If this duty is to be absorbed by the United States producers, so that they can keep the market they have in Canada to-day, how is this going to help the coal producer's in Nova Scotia or even encourage the use of their coal?	.
Let me point out something else. The Prime Minister has just made the statement: "No man will dare say we have not met the situation." That is a point-blank, determined, absolute statement that they have met the situation. Then we have the statement of the Minister of Fisheries: "We have not met the situation as fully as it should be met, but I am convinced that as time goes on this government will meet it."

I have no exception to
take to the latter part of the quotation, but the first portion is not in my words. I never said we had not met the situation.
I did not say that. I said the minister stated: We have not met the situation fully.
If we have not.

I am using (the words of the hon. gentleman. Hansard to-morrow will show who is right. Let me go further. We have the statement of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley), who, speaking on the budget, said that the situation was not met. When he was in opposition he asked 'for $1.50 a ton, and he still believes there should be a higher tariff on importations of bituminous coal; but he was pleased to accept as a beginning what had been given. Place those two statements against those made this afternoon 'by the Prime Minister. No man will dare say that we have failed to meet the situation. Whom are we to believe? The Minister of Fisheries, the member for Pictou, or the Prime Minister of Canada?
Quote the member for Pictou correctly.
I did.

Is not that absolute proof that the hon. gentleman believes that the situation has not been met? If it had been met, why would he make the threat thalt the people of Nova Scotia would come back at a future date and ask for a higher duty on coal? No doubt he expects they will ask for the duty that he asked the Liberal government to puit on, when he was sitting in opposition. He then asked for a duty of $1.50 a ton, and1 he said that the people of Nova Scotia would never be satisfied until they got it. But now he is satisfied with a measly 25 cents of an increase in the tariff.
In closing his remarks the right hon. the Prime Minister, in reply to an interjection that I made, said that was right, that it must be conclusive since I had made the statement. I am glad, Mr. Chairman, that I have been enabled to give something conclusive to the Prime Minister, because since the opening of the session we have not obtained anything from him of a conclusive nature in connection with the tariff. The tariff as introduced on
