I think perhaps I might congratulate myself in at last drawing out the Prime Minister and inducing him to give some reason for the placing of the 40 cent duty on hard coal, even if I did draw upon myself the usual lecture that he administers to those who do not agree with him. That is his invariable custom. I also gave him the opportunity of reflecting rather extravagantly upon myself, because I had not been always in agreement with my colleagues. I suppose it is quite natural for him to be surprised at that, because while he usually boasts of his own frankness he cannot understand that anybody on this side of the house might possess the quality of frankness to the same degree as himself. But I am not going to dwell on these personal matters or speak at length.
I	asked the Prime Minister to give the reason why he placed the duty of 40 cents a ton on hard coal, and to tell the committee how it fits into any scheme for the development of a national fuel policy. I said the other day that the Prime Minister always makes a very good speech when he has a good case, and sometimes a pretty good speech when his case is not so good. His case to-day I think comes within the latter category. He has not to my mind made a case for the placing of 40 cents a ton duty on hard coal. The only attempt he made to show that this duty fits in with the development of a national fuel policy was when he tried to make out that it will mean ultimately -it certainly will not this year or next year-that Alberta coal will be sold in the province of Ontario and thus take the place of hard coal from the United States. He gave another reason, one that I myself suggested last night as possibly having moved him, and that is that it helps in the development of inter-empire trade, that it may bring more Welsh coal to Canada. That, however, I contend is not a factor in the development of a national fuel policy. Lastly, he said that he wanted to encourage the production and consumption of coke in this country. In order for that to fit in with a national fuel policy, it must mean the further development of the coal areas of Nova Scotia and in the west. I say to the Prime Miinster, in just a few words that there is nothing in that argument because just so long as he allows 
United States soft coal to come in here for the purpose of making coke, he is doing nothing to develop the soft coal business of the maritime provinces or of the west.

My right hon. friend as
usual has indulged in a good deal of recrimination, squirming and wriggling, and blustering and scolding, but it does not phase anybody on this side of the house a bit. We are quite used to it, and if the Prime Minister wants to indulge in that sort of thing I suppose that we can. just wait here till he gets over it. What we are dealing with is a particular item of the tariff. I commend his leader's speech to the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. MacDonald) who is so keen on non-partisanship. I commend to him the statements made by the Prime Minister, having nothing whatever to do with this item-in fact, he went out of his way to lecture and criticize members of the former government in connection with the way they administered public affairs generally. But I want to point out to the Prime Minister that after he has gotten all through, we come back to the position from which I began when I made my few remarks. It was this: The Prime Minister said at Inverness that he would undertake to meet this situation. His Minister of Fisheries admits quite frankly that he has not met the situation. The Minister of Fisheries says:	"This is one
step," and then turning to the Prime Minister he said, "I do not think the Prime Minister himself would say that this is the complete national fuel policy, but it is one step in that direction." The hon. member for Cape Breton South said exactly the same thing, but the Prime Minister stands up and says: "No man in this house will undertake to say that we have not met the situation." Then later he interrupts and says, "I did not mean when I said, we will meet the situation, that we would meet it successfully."

I have listened
with a great deal of amusement, and I know the miners of Nova Scotia will read with amusement, the remarks indicating the sudden change of attitude on the part of the hon member for Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). My hon. friend from West Edmonton rose for the purpose of correcting a statement of the Prime Minister to the effect that the government of which my hon. friend formed a part was responsible for the plant at Montreal.

My hon. friend should not have the assistance of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth. The plant was placed on the canal because of a provision made by the government of my hon. friend. The minister's argument is rather far-fetched. The drawback on coke has been in existence for years, and I think it is legitimate, quite irrespective of what he says.

My hon. friend says the
drawback on coke has been in existence for years. It has been in effect for metallurgical coke under item 1019; but the drawback to which I am referring was not put into effect until 1925. Here it is:
Bituminous coal when imported after the 24th day of March, 1925.
That was entirely new, placed there by my hon. friends opposite. It has no reference whatever to the drawback on coal for metallurgical purposes. That has been in the tariff for years.

I take full responsibility for recommending that by-product coke be put in the same category as metallurgical coke. It was done for the purpose of reducing the cost of anthracite coal to the people of the central provinces. Nova Scotia does not produce a pound of anthracite coal, neither does New Brunswick. The establishment of these two plants in Hamilton and in Montreal reduced by $4 per ton the cost of anthracite coal in the central region of Canada.

My hon. friend is going

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the committee will recall that the items which remained were those dealing with the income tax. I do not propose to proceed further with them. I have not been accustomed to trouble this chamber with my personal affairs, but since I have been elected to the positions which I have occupied, either as leader of the opposition or as leader of the government, I have endeavoured to discharge my duties to the best of my ability. I have not thought of my personal fortunes or my personal advancement.
On June 1, I brought before the house proposals with respect to the income tax. I pointed out that in the main they would have no application, so far as revenue was concerned, until next year; they would be applicable then and not now. The usual course adopted by my predecessors has been to bring such measures before the house shortly before the end of the fiscal year so that the taxes would be applicable to that fiscal year and be paid on the rates fixed by the statute passed just prior to its expiration. I thought it well that the house and country should have the fullest opportunity to consider the measure which was submitted, and I

Income War Tax Act
shall now relate to the committee the circumstances under which it was submitted.
As Minister of Finance I realized that I had not the opportunity to study the operations of the Income Tax Act in all its ramifications. The officials of the Income Tax branch are trained men. The commissioner of that branch was appointed to that service by my predecessor. He is a competent official; from the study he has given to the matter he has a wide knowledge, of the operations of income tax legislation in every part of the world. While it has been said that one should not refer to an official in dealing with a matter of this kind, it has always been the custom of those who come and go to ask permanent officials to give, through the legislation framed by them, the benefit of their advice to the country. Accordingly I asked the head of the Income Tax branch to prepare a measure that he believed was the best in the interests of the Dominion of Canada, having regard to his experience, to his knowledge of the operations of similar taxes in other countries, and to what he has learned, on the one hand, as to the ability of our people to pay, and, on the other, of the encouragement of capital. He prepared a bill, and I should like the committee to realize that that bill was submitted to me on the night before the budget was presented. I handed to the clerk at the tabic the very sheets of paper which that official gave to me. It was my intention to have had the resolution passed in the house and to have had the bill referred to the committee on banking and commerce in order that hon. gentlemen might have an opportunity before that committee to question the officials of the department and to determine to what extent the bill as prepared represented what was best in the interests of Canada.
To my surprise I was personally attacked for this measure. If hon. members are interested enough to look at the speech delivered by a former minister of the crown, the ex-Secretary of State, the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), he is reported as saying at page 2778 of Hansard:
If .... he had told the people he was going to raise the sales tax from one per cent to four per cent; that he was going to impose a one per cent tax on all the imports of this country; that he was going to do that most infamous tmng, relieve himself and his wealthy friends Pc1' cent of their income tax, not only would he not have won the election but in certain parts of the country he would have been stoned away from his meetings.
That in the French version is now being circulated throughout the province of Quebec, the interpretation being that by this "infamous" act I reduced by 25 per cent the tax on my own income, and so on.
Another former minister of the crown, Mr. Gordon of Peterborough, made the statement at a public gathering that the proposed income tax would save me $25,000 personally. On the one hand there is the statement made in this chamber that I was legislating to save myself 25 per cent of my income tax; on the other, there is the statement made out of the chamber that I was legislating by lessening my tax to prevent myself paying $25,000. I do not know at the moment what the effect of the proposed income tax legislation would have been upon my personal income tax. I have never been concerned about that. I have always paid with pleasure my income tax, and on three occasions I have been refunded overpayments. I have maintained no corporation; I have set up no personal or family corporation with respect to my affairs. I have paid as an individual I have maintained no trust funds abroad where my income should accumulate and where no income tax would have to be paid on it. But I do not think the committee is concerned about my personal affairs. I defy any man to make about any business of mine with respect to the Dominion of Canada a single criticism that would be warranted or to point to any departure from the letter of the law in favour of myself. Not only are the statements, the one made in the house and the other made. outside, untrue, but I confess when I saw the rancour with which the attacks were made upon me with respect to the matter, I felt that in the public interest I must ask the committee to permit me to withdraw this resolution. The taxes will remain as they are. It does not follow that when the time for payment comes, whoever occupies the position of Minister of Finance may not think some action desirable, for I recall that the leader of the opposition, in addressing the people of Canada at Richmond Hill on September 5, 1925, had this to say.
But is reduction already effected sufficient? Uur income tax is still in some respects higher tban that of the United States. . . . While aiming at a further reduction in the public debt we must aim also at a further reduction m the income tax and the sales tax.
That is from the Globe of Monday, September 7, 1925. I am not now concerned about that matter. This measure did not touch the budget. That is what is the unexplainable point about it. It was introduced with the budget resolutions as a convenient
Income War Tax Act

place to enable the matter to be discussed, and if I ask the tolerance of the committee to make the statement I have made, it is because I have been hurt more than I have been in my life before to think that in a chamber such as this an ex-minister of the crown would charge me with having endeavoured to save myself from paying 25 per cent of my tax; and that out of this chamber a charge should be made that I would endeavour to save myself from paying 525,000. Neither is correct; if it were I should be unworthy of standing in the place I occupy.
I hope that I may be forgiven for touching upon my personal affairs as I have done. How can the state expect men with any means to serve it if their motives must be misconstrued and attacks such as this made upon them? I think in one great country the services of one of its richest men have been given in a way that will be remembered by posterity for a very long time. I have no such hopes in my own case, but I will continue as unselfishly as I know how, to serve Canada that has done so much for me, and I shall endeavour, out of the resources that a kindly Providence has permitted me to have, to make those contributions which the state justly takes. But I shall never become a party to having it thought in the house or by the country that any legislation fathered by me or resolutions moved by me in committee of ways and means have been actuated by any object other than the well-being of my fellow' Canadians. I know not to-night what effect the resolutions would have upon my own fortunes, except that I do know it is absolutely untrue that they would affect my payment of income tax in the manner indicated either in this chamber or outside it.
Once more I ask the tolerance of the committee for having brought to its attention my personal affairs. Hon. gentlemen are not concerned with them except in so far as they touch the state, and if I ask the committee to permit me now to withdraw these resolutions that affect the income tax amendment, I do so in the firm belief that it is my duty under the circumstances to take this course.

I do not know
whether it is in order to make any observations on my right hon. friend's remarks or not. I do not know whether I heard my hon. friend aright, but whether I heard him aright or not, I am going to make some observations if I am in order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Certainly.

On the 15th of June, two weeks after my right hon. friend made

his budget speech, I made my contribution to the budget debate. In the meantime I was very anxious to know what the income tax provisions meant, and I put a question on the order paper asking the Minister of National Revenue what amount of income tax would be collected under the provisions of the new act on a million dollar income, and what amount would be collected on the same income under the old income tax. About ten minutes before I started to speak in the budget debate a copy of the reply of my hon. friend the Minister of National Revenue was handed to me, the substance of which was that inasmuch as there had been no million dollar income taxable property for a number of years, he presumed that I meant the corporation tax, and he gave his answer accordingly. I considered that that was a smart Aleck answer. He was admitting more than he meant to admit, because he admitted right there that there had been some taxable incomes of a million dollars.
Not in recent years. My hon. friend was asking for something that he did not understand. He thought he had something with which to make a case, but he had not.

The very fact that there had been such incomes indicated the necessity of having the schedule. The income tax schedule was available to anybody at the office. There was no secret about it. Anybody could get it. The schedules indicated that on incomes from $3,500 to $8,000 there was a reduction of tax, on incomes from $8,000 to $137,000 an increase, and on incomes from $137,000 to $1,000,000 a decrease in the income tax. Those who were fortunate enough to hold taxable income property above $137,000 paid under the new act less income taxation than under the old. I did not know who had incomes above $137,000. I understood that there were about sixty individuals in Canada with incomes above that, and I took the ground and I take it now, that this is not the time for the man who had an income above $137,000 to unload any part of his former income tax on the poor people of Canada. As I say, there were a few incomes from $3,500 to $8,000 on which the income tax was reduced, the reduction amounting in the aggregate to about $50 a year. That is my recollection; I have not the figures before me. There were some sixty people who had taxable income property between $137,000 and $1,000,000. Who they are I do not know, but whoever they are my remarks applied to them, and they still apply to them.

Income War Tax Act

Needless
to say, it is always best to be discreet and await an explanation of any legislation that is introduced. I confess that I heard a good deal about the reductions in income taxation. I presumed that we would discuss it when the legislation came before the house, but now we shall have no opportunity as the Prime Minister desires to withdraw the resolution. I think it is regrettable in public life that one is always subjected to suspicion. Tihat is something that my right hon. friend is just beginning to realize now after many years of public service. As head of the government he will be subjected to all sorts of suspicions, but I would say to him as an old friend and former colleague that I would not feel too badly about it. One has to put up with that sort of thing. It is part of the penalty we pay for being in public life. One is bound to be attacked from every quarter. I am bound to say that in some twenty odd years, holding positions of some responsibility, I have sometimes been pained at the suggestions I have heard against my honesty and integrity, and in the higher position my right hon. friend occupies one can readily understand that he will be always subjected to criticism. I am going to say now, notwithstanding that he has withdrawn the resolutions; that I think it would have been much better had he gone through with them. I do not know what effect thiey would have or what changes they would bring about, but as my right hon. friend feels as he does about the matter and has withdrawn the resolutions, I do not suppose there is anything more to be said about it.
Shall the right hon. gentleman have leave to withdraw his resolution?

speechtext:

With respect to the two per cent tax the reason for withdrawing it is fairly clear under present conditions. Repercussions of the present conditions in Canada began to be realized fully after the middle of June, and it is the most inopportune time in the world to present such a resolution in view of these repercussions in Europe, as may be found from a perusal of the Times and continental papers of repute in Paris and elsewhere. I will admit further that it

If the changes that were proposed, and which the Prime Minister feels may be presumed to affect him personally, were changes which were right, I think it is still his duty to press through that legislation. While I am perfectly free to admit that the Prime Minister has a very fine sense of honour, perhaps he is exaggerating the effect

so far as he is personally affected by the proposed change. I repeat, if the Prime Minister is now convinced, if he was not before, and the committee is convinced, that the changes proposed in the income tax are such as are right in every way and can be properly defended, then I believe in justice to the Canadian people and to other income taxpayers than himself, the Prime Minister ought to press the legislation through. At the same time I quite understand the feeling that influenced him because of certain criticisms which were made. As Prime Minister and Minister of Finance my right hon. friend has a great responsibility. I would make the statement, not by way of criticism, that his responsibility goes far beyond any personal feeling he may have.

I cannot view with equanimity the thought that in every back concession, every comer lot, every grocery store and every libellous and scurrilous sheet statements are being made that I have done so and so for my own personal advantage. I submit to the committee that it would have been improper for me to do the arithmetic for the ex-Minister of Agriculture when in fact there was no person in the Dominion in receipt of an income of 81,000,000 or paying taxes thereon. There was no one last year paying taxes on that amount, nor on 8750,000. While on my feet I remember that there were two who paid a tax on 8500,000. What was the purpose of the ex-Minister of Agriculture asking the amount of taxation on 81,000.000 under the old rates and under the proposed rates when as a matter of fact in the whole Dominion of Canada there was no such case. I think it may be said that an honest answer was given to a smart Aleck question.

There was no reason under the sun why my hon. friend should not have answered the question as to what was the difference between the tax on 81,000,000 under the new and old systems. There is no reason why the minister could not have answered my question. When I asked the question he had no right to assume that I meant anything about the corporation tax, and for him to make such a reply was a downright insult. It was nothing but a smart Aleck answer I received from my hon. friend.
I did not quite gather from the remarks of the Minister of Finance whether that seotion dealing with the exemptions of $3,000 being raised to $3,500 is to be proceeded with or not.

It would be rather awkward for the government and parliament if legislation were to be affected because of warranted or unwarranted attacks lodged against the Prime Minister or any other public man.
Hear, hear.

Personally I should have been the last to feel that the Prime Minister would have thought of himself when proposing any legislation of this kind. On the other hand, under the circumstances and because of public discussions which take place throughout the country, he must not be surprised if some comments are passed. I well remember the time when his predecessor in office

and that lasted a good many years- went through various elections facing charges of cowardice and lack of patriotism because he did not choose to enlist during the war. I respectfully suggest to the right hon. gentleman that in this respect as in all othef respects he frame his mind, propose his policy and propound it before parliament and before the country, irrespective of any personal comments that may be made by this or that gentleman inside or outside the house. Income War Tax Act

Quite so, and on the
whole I approve of the government withdrawing these resolutions. But I say, if in the future any prime minister should come to a decision to withdraw certain measures because of personal attacks made upon him by some of his opponents, I think it would be detrimental to the course of legislation and to the proper administration of the country's affairs. If the accusation is false, then it falls of itself; if it is brought in such a manner outside of parliament that the Prime Minister or any other member of his government or of the house is capable of bringing before the tribunals of the country those who accuse him falsely, then, like any other citizen, he has recourse in law against his traducers. But to say ithat legislation should be changed because of personal attacks on a minister of the crown is, I think, pretty far-fetched and it seems to me it would ibe a very dangerous precedent. The right hon. gentleman could well have stated his personal position without taking the course that he has taken because of the attack, in which so far as I am concerned I do not believe at all.

As is usually the case, I think mokt of us view this action with mingled feelinga Speaking for myself-and I think a great many other people-I would say this. To the extent that the proposed measures increased the income tax, we regret their withdrawal; tto the extent that they lessened -the income tax, whether at the top or the bottom, some of us, including myself, approve of their withdrawal. So far as the personal element is concerned, may I also say that although some of us may not agree with the Prime Minister's general policy, I think there are few of us 'but recognize that the Prime Minister, whether right or wrong in his policy, is too 'big a man to allow personal considerations to interfere with the performance of his duty; and that while we disapprove of the suggestion to reduce the income tax upon the larger incomes, we do not believe for one moment that these measures were introduced from any personal motive or from the point of view of the manner in which they might affect the Prime Minister's own personal fortune. I repeat, whether we agree or disagree with him, we regard him as too big a man to allow such considerations to affect his conduct.

speechtext: It does matter.

The point is that, owing
largely to his friends, the right hon. gentleman has the reputation in this country of being a man of great wealth. It was perhaps fair on the part of the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rin-fret) to assume that the right hon. gentleman would be one of those whose incomes would have been to a certain extent exempted from taxation by these proposals. I do not know whether or not it would have been. I have no means of finding out, nor do I care. But if that were the fact-and we have been assured that the right hon. gentleman is a man of great wealth-I think it .was possible, without making any personal

Income War Tax Act
reflection on the right hon. gentleman-and so far as I am concerned personally he knows I have not the slightest inclination to do so -that if as a matter of fact he had an income in excess of 3130,000 a year, by the act of this government he would pay less m the way of income tax than he otherwise would have done. I think that is a fair statement to make.
Now, I am extremely sorry that the right hon. Prime Minister took this attack to himself. It is inevitable in the political life of this or any other country that one's motives should be misjudged. I do not think any cne on this side of the house would deliberately say that the Prime Minister in the exercise of the functions of Minister of Finance which he has assumed would have introduced this legislation for the purely selfish motive of diminishing his own income tax. I think all hon. members on this side of the house will back me up when I make that statement on their behalf, and so far as 1 am concerned T make it gladly and willingly. I do believe that the very last thing which would have entered into the mind of the right hon. Prime Minister would be to secure any personal advantage to himself. But that having been said-
Bluff.

There is no question of bluff. I have been in the habit of speaking frankly and honestly in this house, and I will do so now. But that having been said, with all due regard to the sensibilities and susceptibilities of my right hon. friend, I do not believe it is either fair or reasonable on his part to withdraw the really beneficial clauses in this legislation because he felt that he had been personally attacked.

speechtext:
I did not even re-read
the copy of Hansard.

I do not doubt that if the right hon. gentleman had gone through it he would have found it most interesting reading. I wish he would read it now. There is a heading:
Financial operations during fiscal year 1930-31.
That is one chapter, a part of the budget speech; and I will guarantee, without knowing anything about it, that if this speech has been distributed to the right hon. gentleman's friends it is in this very shape. Then there is another heading, "Excise Duty," and a third section under the heading "Income Tax." The text reads:
The income tax ranks first in productivity,
And so forth. It goes on:
The fiscal year 1922 was also a dark one in respect to total revenues, but income tax assessments were on the earnings and profits of 1920, the peak year of the post-war boom. In the past year total revenues were again reduced, but income tax assessments were levied on the earnings and profits of a peak year, that of the stock market boom.
He goes on to describe the financial operations, and later on he says:
I may add that it is proposed also during the present session entirely to amend the Income Tax Act. Family corporations will be abolished; it is about time.
Income War Tax Act

There is still time; why have we not done it? He continues:
In addition to that we propose to present a new schedule of rates based upon the experience of the commissioner of taxation. Mr. Walters was asked to prepare, with the aid of his officials, what he conceived to he a proper tax rate for this country, having regard to known conditions. He has done so, and the government proposes to adopt his recommendations.
The foregoing appears at page 2174 of Hansard of June 1. Could any language be plainer than that? The government knew what Mr. Walters' recommendations were, and they proposed to adopt them. The right hon. gentleman goes on to say:
The exemptions will be somewhat increased, hut it is thought desirable that the rate should start at 1 per cent, with another 1 per cent added with each additional $1,000 of income until the maximum is reached, which will be 25 per cent.
Then he goes on:
It may amaze the house to learn .... that the amount of income tax collected in this country since the tax first was put on the statute hooks-
-was so and so. Then he proceeds:
In addition it is proposed that dividends from Canadian corporations, up to $10,000, shall be exempt from taxation. . . .
And he goes on further to describe and to elaborate upon his income tax proposals.
Now, the fault I have to find with the right hon. gentleman is this, to put it very plainly and in very few words: that because he felt aggrieved at being attacked in the house and in the country-and perhaps I am not blaming him for that.-he has disregarded entirely those sections of the income tax amendments which would have brought considerable benefit to certain classes in the country who are badly in need of it.
Badly in need.

Will the hon. gentleman who interrupts say that the classes of people who under this proposed legislation would have benefited by an increase of 8500 in exemption are not badly in need of it? If any hon. gentleman says so, he does not know the feelings of the people. It is to that class of people particularly that I refer, and I deeply regret the action taken by the Prime Minister. I would ask him, if possible, to reconsider the matter.
Is it the pleasure of the committee that the right hon. gentleman shall have leave to withdraw the resolutions?

Carried.

Mr. 'Chairman, this item
is subdivided into other items which include salaries and allowances; mail service, including mail service by air; miscellaneous expenditures, and so on, about fourteen different items in all. I thought we were to take the items up separately, but before going into the discussion of any item in detail, I wish to direct the attention of the committee to the time these estimates were last before it on Tuesday last. On that occasion the item taken up was Salaries, and the minister made a statement to t.he house reviewing the administration of the department for the year ended March 31, 1931. As soon as the minister finished I called the attention of the chairman to the fact that I thought the minister had gone out of his way to make a Statement under a civil government item which should properly have been made under an outside or general administration item. At that time I claimed the right of replying to the hon. gentleman at such time as we might reach the first item, and the chairman stated that this permission would be granted in view of the fact that the minister had made an extended statement without having gone into the details of any item. With the indulgence of the committee, I now propose to reply to the statement made by the minister.
In doing this it will be necessary to refer to many figures, and I intend to confine myself to a large extent to the notes and figures which I have before me. In reviewing the administration of his department, and in dealing with the deficit of approximately $5,000,006 for the year ended March 31, 1931, the minister said:	'	[DOT]
The deficit which has occurred in the department is due to the decrease of revenue brought about by the crisis affecting this and other

Supply-Post Office
countries of the world, while the increase in expenditure is caused by the obligations for the development of service imposed upon the department by the former administration and authorized by previous parliaments.
The admission that the world-wide depression is the cause of a great part of this deficit is a source of gratification to myself. A provincial election is being carried on in Prince Edward Island, and the papers which support the federal government are stating that the increase in postage has been necessitated by the maladministration of the former Postmaster General. We now have the admission by the present Postmaster General that the falling off in revenue, amounting to approximately $2,000,000, has been caused, not by the maladministration of the former Postmaster General, but by the world-wide depression which has affected every branch of the public service. I want to thank the Postmaster General for affording me an opportunity of showing that this deficit was not brought about-he has never made this accusation- by the maladministration of the department when I had the honour to preside over it.
The minister informed the committee that the decrease in revenue due to the world-wide depression amounted to $2,000,000, and I desire to draw the attention of the committee to what would have been the finances of the Post Office Department if there had not been a world-wide depression. If the revenue had increased in the year ended March 31, 1931, in proportion to the increases shown in the years 1928-29 and 1929-30, the net revenue for 1931 would have been $34,767,680 instead of $31,000,000. The Postmaster General gave the increases in revenue for the years 1928 and 1929, which show that the normal annual increase of revenue ranged from $1,500,000 to as high as $1,750,000. We were told by the minister that the increased expenditure in 1930-31 as compared with 1929-30 amounted to $1255,974, which would make the expenditure for 1930-31, $30292,603 All things being equal and with no world-wide depression, the net deficit for 1930-31, based on the proportionate increases for the previous years, would have been only $1,524,923 instead of approximately $5,000,000. This net deficit of $1,524,923 would represent just about the amount expended upon air mail service. It will be remembered by hon. members who sat in the house in 1929 that when as Postmaster General I submitted my estimates at that time, we fully discussed the question whether the administration of the Post Office should be one that would bring about surpluses or would be such as to give the greatest amount of service to the people and at the same time
make both ends meet. Members of all groups in the house agreed at the time that no attempt should be made to run the Post Office Department on the basis of surpluses, and that should any surpluses occur, they should be used for the betterment of the service throughout the Dominion.
On that occasion I made the statement that if the revenues should continue to be buoyant as they were in 1927 and 1928 and prior to the end of March, 1929, I had every reason to expect that by the end of the fiscal year 1930 we would be able to make both ends meet, leaving out of the picture the air mail service, which had been inaugurated the year before. The statement submitted by the Postmaster General the other evening bears out the prediction I made at that time; if no world wide depression had struck Canada, the revenues of the Post Office Department would have continued to increase year after year as they had done prior to the end of the fiscal year 1929, and all things being equal, at the end of 1930 the Post Office Department would have been in a position to make both ends meet. That being the case, I fail to see where it can be charged that the present deficit is attributable to any maladministration on the part of the former Postmaster General or his officials. Notwithstanding the fact that in 1926, before I assumed the position of Postmaster General, the rate of postage on letters had been reduced from three to two cents, thereby naturally, one would think, causing a reduction in the revenues of the department, by 1928. The expansion in the volume of business effected by that reduction and the progressive state of affairs in Canada brought about such an increase in the revenue of the department that it still kept above what it had been at the time the reduction was made.
The minister in his statement the other night told the committee of the necessity of making certain curtailments in the postal service of the Dominion. May I say how deeply I regret the curtailment of the general mail service as indicated on that occasion by the minister. In view of the largely increased revenue which must come from the higher rate of postage in connection with first-and second-class matter, and the increased revenue that will be derived from the extra sale of postage stamps to be placed on postal notes, money orders, and cheques, all of which will reach the sum of at least $4,000,000 after the provisions have been in operation for a year, and in view of the contemplated rearrangement of the air mail service as indicated by the minister, there is no need of such curtail-
Supply-Post Office

ments as are being made; and especially is there no need for cutting from the railway mail service the sum of $35,000 as indicated by the estimates submitted to the house and referred to by the minister the other day.
The minister told the committee that the curtailment of railway mail service was brought about by certain changes in the hours, in the operations of trains and so forth. That is quite true. When I was Postmaster General the same changes were made in the summer time, but it must not be forgotten that when summer changes in the railway time tables bring about a curtailment of railway mail service, the department has to supplement the loss occasioned by that curtailment by the use of highway communication and other means of giving to the public the daily service they received when the trains were running regularly. When the railway service, as occurs in many cases, is reduced from daily to three times a week, the department cannot leave the mail service at only three times a week between the points affected. If they cannot give the service by rail, they must supplement it by highway or steamboat communication- the service must be maintained. I am not saying that the service has not bean maintained, but it is no excuse to say that the estimates' should be cut down because of changes in railway communication.
The policy adopted by the minister not to increase the mail train service will, I hope, not be put into effect. What is understood by not increasing the railway mail service is that in future there shall be no extension of services by rail or what is known as railway post offices to cities or districts which, with largely increasing populations, must have that service if they wish to keep up with progress. To close up the very necessary service which is known as the railway post office system is detrimental to the progress of the districts interested. Therefore I claim that the minister should not, and I hope he will not, refuse to give those extensions where the business of the country warrants them, even if this should bring about a deficit in his department. I appeal to the minister not to put that policy into effect except in cases where he finds it absolutely essential so to do. Let me add this to what I have already said in this respect: this service plays a large part in establishing better industrial conditions. I hope the government has not lost faith in the country to such an extent that because of the depression which has struck Canada we are going to curtail a service which will help in the future that industrial development so necessary under present conditions.

Another statement made by the minister was that (he rural sections cannot expect any extension. Here again I would express the hope that he will see his way clear not to put that into effect. This service is one of the most important of the whole mail service, and no matter what the economic conditions may be, our rural population should not be sidetracked for the sake of practising small economies.
The minister tells us further that the increase in expenditure is caused by the obligations for development of service imposed upon the department by the former administration and authorized by previous parliaments. I am free, Mr. Chairman, to admit that to a great extent this is quite true. Certain obligations were undertaken which must now be carried out, but will the minister and his colleagues in the government claim that the department should have remained still and not have tried to meet the various demands made upon it for improved services, especially in the far-flung areas of Canada, for the opening up of new territory, for better rural mail service-which was to a great extent inaugurated under the administration of your humble servant-and for better train mail service? I appeal to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). Would he find any fault-I am sure he would not- with the attitude of the department in bringing about improvements and efficiency in the train mail service and other mail services that we provided at large expense throughout British Columbia and sections of the territories, such as the Mackenzie valley, the district of Vermilion, and other districts that I could name, where at large expense the department undertook to give the people the service to which they were entitled, and for the lack of which not only had they been suffering individually, but the districts concerned had been handicapped in their industrial development?
Can fault be found because we gave better accommodation for the urban mail service? Will the members representing Toronto, Winnipeg, Montreal and other cities undertake to criticize the late administration and the Post Office Department for the magnificent extra service that was provided during my regime? Toronto, under the regime of your humble servant, was given a postal service and postal facilities unequalled on the continent of America, and that service was inaugurated in the main during the time your humble servant was head of that department. It cost money to do it, but parliament agreed to it. Everything was laid before parliament, and parlia-

Supply-Post Office
ment was satisfied and willing that these improvements should be made.
Vast improvements were also made in the sub-postal service in the city of Montreal, and improvements weTe contemplated for the future in order to place Montreal on the same basis as Toronto. That system was started under your humble servant, and I hope the minister will see his way clear to carry out what was started in 1929. I hope he will not neglect the city of Montreal, that he will accommodate the people of that city with a better service than they have to-day, and that there will be no neglect because the government wishes to practise small economies. I trust that the improvements at Montreal will be gone on with, so that Montreal may be placed on the same footing as Toronto. True, it will cost money both to the Post Office Department and the Department of Public Works, but when that work is done you will have two of the largest cities in Canada occupying a position in mail service distribution that it will be difficult to equal in any part of the wide world. That is saying a great deal, but that Canada in its system of mail distribution stands to-day ahead of any other country in the world cannot be gainsaid. Not only do we stand ahead of any other country in our system of mail distribution by land and by sea, by rail and by boat, but we stand also at the head of the great American republic in the system that we have inaugurated for the distribution of mail by air. I shall not at the moment go into the details of the distribution of mail by air. I shall reserve my right to deal with that when the item touching the air mail service is before us for consideration. I shall then undertake to prove to the committee, and to convince them if it is possible, and the government of the day, that they would be making the greatest mistake if they curtailed the mail service by air to such an extent as to cripple what is becoming one of the most important mail services in the Dominion of Canada.
I was referring to obligations that had been imposed upon the government in my time, and will now have to be carried out by the department under its present administration. Yes, there were obligations undertaken, others than those I have mentioned. Take for instance the obligation of increasing the salaries and allowances of tlhe rural postmasters in my time, amounting to practically 8700,000 or 8800,000 a year. Take the obligation of the increased remuneration of the railway mail clerks, amounting to somewhere in the vicinity of 8150,000 or 8160,000. Take the obligation imposed by the Civil Service Act
of statutory increases, amounting to practically 8200,000 per year. Take the obligation imposed under the Civil Service Act again of increases given to the inside service at the rate of 8120 a year in some cases, and in other cases at the rate of 860 a year, amounting in all during the last three years of my administration of that department to at least $1,500,000. Had the government adopted a niggardly policy in connection with these matters, no increases would have been given to the postmasters in the rural districts, no increases would have been given to the railway mail clerks, and the department would have opposed the bulk sum of increases under the Civil Service Act. But. no, we felt that these men deserved the increases they got. If these increases had not been granted, and we had gone on following in the ordinary course, there would have been no deficit in the department at the end of 1930, instead of a deficit amounting to around 81,500,000. The department in 1929, and before that date, would have been able to make both ends meet, even including the air mail service expenditure. But we accepted those obligations, and I know that no member on either side of the house will undertake to blame the late administration for having given these increases in salaries and allowances. I feel I can stand before this committee and the country and rejoice in the fact that I was able at that time, owing to the condition of affairs, to give those increases.
Right here may I correct a statement the minister made the other night. I know his error was not voluntary because I have faith in his integrity, although I may not have a great deal of faith in Conservative administration of the department. I knew he would not willingly make a misstatement to the house. Dealing with the question of reductions in postage the minister stated that the reduction for Canada took place in 1926 and that in the same year a reduction took place on mail rates to the British empire. The reduction in the British empire postage did not take place until December 25, 1928. In order that the record may be clear I wish to make that correction.
The minister made the following statement:
Notwithstanding the decrease in revenue, all services have been maintained, existing services have been extended and new services inaugurated. The increase in expenditure cannot be said to be due to the present administration but rather to the extensive nature of the service accorded to the public.
I refer the committee to the words:
All services have been maintained, existing services have been extended and new services inaugurated.
Supply-Post Office

If I am correctly informed the demands for the inauguration of new services have been consistently turned down by the minister and his department. I fail to see where under his administration new services have been inaugurated. But if they were; and he attempted to take credit for them, how can he blame the old government for the total over-expenditure which has taken place since he assumed charge of the department? He who would eat the pudding should have it laid on his table at noon time each day; once it is eaten, however, it is gone. Therefore the minister cannot blame the old government for the entire over-expenditure and at the same time claim credit for inauguration of new services. May I say I have no apology to offer either for the obligation placed upon the country when I was Postmaster General, or for the obligations which the new Postmaster General had to assume when he took office. My only hope now is that the Postmaster General will continue the policies inaugurated by myself and the officials who so faithfully worked under me. I suggest that he continue to extend those services in Canada, notwithstanding the fact that he may fear a deficit; as the country grows, extension of mail services will help to bring about the change in economic conditions so much desired at the present time. My experience of four years in the administration of the Post Office Department has convinced me that there is not another branch of the public service which contributes so much to the expansion of industry and commerce as does the mail service, if properly administered.
The minister told the committee also that the reduction in postal rates made at various times during the regime of the former government has caused a reduction in revenue. It is true that when the postage was reduced the revenue became less. If it had not been reduced I believe the revenue would have been greater at the end of 1927 than it was at the end of 1926. As I pointed out a few minutes ago, however, notwithstanding the reduction the revenue increased by volume of business to such an extent that in the years 1928, 1929 and 1930 they exceeded those of the year in which the reduction was made from three to two cents. The estimates now before the house contain more reductions than those submitted to the house by the department when I was at its head.
I do not intend to take up more time of the committee in this general statement, but shall confine myself to an analysis of the various items as they are called, and especially those which show a reduction this year as compared with last year.

I note you are under the impression that he was dismissed on recommendation of Mr. Bird, M.P. This is not the case, as Mr. Bird had nothing to do with it. The dismissal was made on the recommendation of the executive of the Liberal association. I do not see how I could now reinstate him.
Yours very truly,
P. J. Veniot.

Since I came to Ottawa I have written several letters myself in an effort to find out the reason for this man's dismissal. I appreciate the fact that since a new postmaster has been appointed it would be rather a hardship to let him go in order to put Mr. Hrushowy back on the job, but in justice to a man who has served for fifteen years, I think the reason for his dismissal should be given.
Mr. Bird, my predecessor, did not make any objection to this man, and the letter of the Postmaster General states quite frankly that the dismissal was made at the request of the Liberal association. Does the committee consider that this man has received a fair deal? Again I suggest to the present Postmaster General that he should not follow in the footsteps of the former incumbent of that office.

Mr. Chairman, if I may revert for a moment to the item before the committee, I wish to direct attention to a situation which has arisen in the province of Alberta. In this connection I have had some correspondence with t/he Postmaster General (IMr. Sauve), and I believe he is familiar with the facts. This situation arises through the application of the minimum wage law, to the assistants employed by the postmasters in the small towns throughout the [DOT] province. While most of us are distinctly in favour of a minimum wage, we must realize the effect which this act must have upon postmasters whose salaries are based upon a totally different principle. In many cases the application of the act has doubled the remuneration received by these girls, as well as shortened the hours of work. I have no complaint to make with respect to minimum wage laws, nor do I think these girls are receiving too much, but the committee will readily see that it places the postmasters in a very difficult position. I believe that the Postmaster General is familiar with this matter, and that it is being taken into consideration with a view to seeing whether something cannot be done to meet the situation. I urge that action be taken.
There is another matter to which I would direct attention, one of general application which has some connection with what I have just .mentioned. I have received numerous requests from postmasters located in the smaller points who receive very low salaries and are dependent upon commissions on sales of stamps for the larger part of their remuneration. They are very anxious to know what policy will be followed now that a three cent rate has been pilt into force- 
what percentage of commission will be paid, whether it will remain the same as it was under the two cent rate, and how soon, if changes are to be made, they may expect them. In other words they would like to know how soon they may have some reasonable understanding as to their probable income during the coming year. I should be glad if the minister could make some statement on that point. As I say, I am speaking at the request of a number of the postmasters, particularly at smaller points, who have written to me in respect of both these questions.

They will be treating the minister more fairly if they do not make these interjections, because the more they call "carried" the more I will oppose it. I have privileges as a member and I do not think it helps the minister at all for hon. members opposite to keep on interrupting by calling "carried."
In reply to the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Stitt) and his expressed wish that the present Postmaster General shall not follow along the lines adopted by the former one in the matter of dismissals, I have just a word to say. I occupied the position of Postmaster General from the 26th day of September, 1926, to the 7th or 8th day of August, 1930.
Too long.

It may have been too
long, but I may tell the hon. member who interrupts me that he never applied to my department without getting a fair deal. The only thing I hope for is that he will get as fair a deal from the present Postmaster General as he did from me, although he does not deserve it.

The Postmaster General wants to know how many postmasters I dismissed in the province of Quebec in the first ten months I was in office. I have not the figures in detail here, but I can tell him this, that during the first seventeen months I was in office there were 115 dismissals in the province of Quebec, and during the first ten months that my hon. friend has occupied the position of Postmaster General the number of dismissals in the province of Quebec was 99. So we are not running too far apart after all.
The item we are discussing is No. 358. I want to call the attention of the Postmaster General to what I think is an error in the estimates, so that he may look into the matter to-morrow and have the error corrected or an explanation made-a correction will facilitate the passing of the estimates. The estimate submitted by the Postmaster General this year for stationery and printing is $490 000, and in the comparative column for 1930-31, the last year I was in office, the estimate for that year is given as $865,623. The only estimate submitted to the house by me at that time was $490,000. The explanation may be that included in that $865,623 is an amount of $375,623 for the payment of back debts due the printing establishment. If that explanation is correct I would point out that that $375,623 was voted in the supplementary estimates at the opening of parliament in March of this year, and has no right to appear as an estimate submitted by me to the house for 1930-31. But by including it in the estimates that I submitted to the house for 193031, it is made to appear that there is a reduction as between the present estimate and 
the estimate I submitted last year of $375,623, which is misleading. I think the explanation is that this $865,623 includes the amount I have mentioned for printing and stationery which was accumulating over several years. I have no objection to that amount being paid, but I do object to the record being falsified as it is-perhaps not intentionally, but the record is wrong as it stands; for I never submitted to the committee of supply for the year 1930-31 the amount of $865,623. The only amount I submitted for printing and stationary was $490,000. I would like the minister to look into the matter and let us have his version of it to-morrow.
As I said at the opening of my remarks tonight, the vote now before the committee, Mr. Chairman, is a bulk vote comprising twelve or fourteen different items, and there are various matters to be discussed under it. We must have an opportunity of going into the details, and while the minister could not reasonably have expected the vote to pass in bulk to-night, he must not be disappointed that none of his estimates have been adopted at this sitting. I have had the experience, which I hope the present minister never will have, of sitting for nineteen days before I could get a single item through. We do not intend to hold the minister that long; whatever criticism may be offered this session will be, so far as I am concerned, friendly criticism. If I have any blame to place on the department for not carrying out certain things which hon. gentlemen opposite advocated when in opposition I am not going to blame the present minister, but I am going to criticize the present Minister of Justice, the Minister of Railways and Canals, the Minister of Public Works and the Prime Minister, who when in opposition demanded such enormous changes from your humble servant and pledged themselves to carry them out if they ever came into office; but to-day they are as dumb as oysters. I see nothing in the estimates with regard to these things. I am not going to criticize the Postmaster General for that, but I am going to condemn others.
Item stands.
